title: Avoidable loss and mitigation
summary: Mitigation limits recovery for loss the injured party could reasonably have avoided after breach. It ordinarily concerns the recoverable amount rather than imposing a separate duty to perform for the breacher’s benefit.
notes:
Rockingham asks why a contractor continued construction after learning that the county repudiated. Parker asks whether a discharged performer had to accept a different proposed role to reduce her damages. Avoidance may require reasonable steps, but not every alternative is sufficiently comparable or reasonable. The breacher’s burden of proving avoidable loss and the factual posture matter.

Identify when the injured party learned of the breach, what alternatives were actually available, their costs and risks, and whether accepting them would sacrifice a protected interest. Distinguish replacement income that truly substitutes for the lost transaction from income that could have been earned in addition to it. The assigned materials also consider arguments about the breacher’s equal opportunity to prevent loss; they do not state a universally accepted exception.

textbookImport.basis: Plain-language synthesis of the cited casebook passages; subject to the jurisdictional and source limits stated there.

topics.mitigation: Recoverable damages exclude loss reasonably avoidable under the governing rule.
